Halifax Examiner

Nova Scotia's independent, adversarial news site

Last week, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced that his government was eliminating the Canadian Ombudsperson for Responsible Enterprise (CORE), an office set up in 2019 by Trudeau’s Liberals.

The CORE was supposed to help ensure Canadian companies working abroad – mining, oil and gas, garment-makers – do not abuse human rights, and do not cause physical, environmental, economic, mental or social harm, or use forced labour.

As the Halifax Examiner reported here, from the start, critics argued that the CORE could not do its job of holding Canadian companies to account by investigating complaints because it was missing subpoena powers and the legal clout to ensure that companies found to be abusing human rights received no funding from agencies like Export Development Canada, and no support from diplomatic missions.

The ombudsperson position has been vacant since April 2025, and the CORE was never given the powers it needed to be effective, despite years of pleading from non-governmental organizations, civil society groups, and even the United Nations.

Bizarrely, Carney used the CORE’s ineffectiveness as an excuse to just eliminate it altogether.

For the many people and groups who worked long and hard for years to get the Canadian government to finally acknowledge that some Canadian extractive companies were committing atrocities around the world, and to set up a federal watchdog where affected communities could file complaints, Carney’s decision to cut rather than strengthen the CORE came as a blow.

Related: ‘Canada, come get your people’: Namibian communities reported abuses to the human rights watchdog Canada built. Two years later, the complaint is still unanswered and the office is gone.

The Canadian Network for Corporate Accountability, which was instrumental in that process, issued a powerful statement the day CBC broke the news that Carney was eliminating the CORE.

“The Canadian Network on Corporate Accountability (CNCA) strongly denounces the Government of Canada’s recent decision to eliminate the Office of the Canadian Ombudsperson for Responsible Enterprise (CORE),” read the statement. “In our view, this represents an abandonment of basic human rights principles, leaving communities and workers who allege serious human rights abuse by Canadian companies at significant risk of further harm.”

The statement continued:

During a press conference, Prime Minister Carney justified the government’s decision by pointing to criticism of the CORE’s ineffectiveness, a concern raised by Canadian civil society groups since the earliest days of the office. Yet the solution has always been to reinforce the office, not eliminate it.

When the CORE was first created, the government announced it would have much-needed independent investigatory powers, as human rights groups and tens of thousands of individual Canadians across the country advocated for. These commitments were abandoned soon after, and the office was later left to languish for over two years without a permanent leader. It appears the CORE was always set up to fail.

It wasn’t just civil society groups that spent years struggling to have the Canadian government create an effective office that could investigate Canadian companies abusing human rights overseas.

Former Liberal MP for Scarborough-Guildwood John McKay, who represented that constituency from 1997 until 2025 when he decided not to run again, also went to great lengths to get such an office set up, and to make Canadian extractive companies working abroad accountable in Canada.

Following on the success of his private member’s bill, the 2008 Official Development Assistance Accountability Act, that stipulates Canadian aid must reduce poverty, reflect the perspectives of the poor, and align with international human rights, in 2010, McKay tabled another one, Bill C-300, called the Corporate Accountability of Mining, Oil and Gas Corporations in Developing Countries Act.

Had it passed, Bill C-300 would have promoted “environmental best practices” and ensured “the protection and promotion of international human rights standards in respect of the mining, oil or gas activities of Canadian corporations in developing countries.” It would also have given the ministers of Foreign Affairs and of International Trade the responsibility “to issue guidelines that articulate corporate accountability standards for mining, oil or gas activities.”

At the time, Stephen Harper’s Conservatives had a minority government, and McKay’s responsible mining bill didn’t pass. It was nearly a decade later, after the United Nations had issued several warnings to Canada about human rights violations by Canadian extractive companies, that the Liberal government of Justin Trudeau finally set up the CORE office.

At the time, McKay told parliament:

Mr. Speaker, nine years ago this month, I introduced a bill on corporate accountability, Bill C-300. It proposed the withdrawal of consular and financial support from Canadian mining companies found to have breached international human rights or environmental standards. Companies told us that this would be the end of western civilization as we knew it. Hell hath no fury like a mining company cut off from its money and support.

Needless to say, Bill C-300 nearly died several times as it made its way from the House to committee and back again. However, die it ultimately did by six votes. However, it had an afterlife and lived on in the imagination of civil society, the international press, and hundreds of thousands of Canadians. At one point, 450,000 petitions were presented to the former prime minister, and ignored.

January 17 was resurrection day for Bill C-300, with the announcement of the creation of the Canadian ombudsperson for responsible enterprise.

I would like to thank the Prime Minister, the previous and current ministers of international trade, and the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who kept the dream of Bill C-300 alive.

Now, seven years later, the CORE is dead.

The Halifax Examiner spoke with John McKay about his long struggle to have the CORE established, why he thinks Canadians should care about it, and about the news that Mark Carney, whom McKay describes as “a friend,” was eliminating it. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

We hope you're enjoying our work. If you'd like to support us with a donation or recurring subscription, please use these buttons. We really appreciate it.

Joan Baxter (JB): What was your reaction when you heard the news that the Canadian Ombudsperson for Responsible Enterprise (CORE) was being cut?

John McKay (JM): Disappointed. It’s short-sighted, is my quick reaction. I’m not surprised. It had been on life support for months, and in fact some would argue, it was set up to fail. I wasn’t quite in that camp. But without powers to investigate and to access and seize documents, and do proper investigations, it [the CORE] could be just blown off and sent in an endless circle of non sequiturs. I’m disappointed that the government didn’t give it the authority and power it should have had. I’m not surprised that when Sheri Meyerhoffer [the first ombudsperson] finished her term, she wasn’t replaced. And in some respects, all this is like having a funeral after a dead body.

JB: Why do you think the CORE was never given the powers to compel documents and testimony from companies?

JM: Well, the people that opposed not only my [private member’s] Bill C-300, but pretty well any accountability regime of any kind, whether it was through a private member’s bill or a government organization or whatever, are pretty influential people and they don’t appreciate having to explain themselves to others. I suspect that you can never underestimate the power of the mining industry, in particular.

JB: When the CORE was announced in 2019, you told parliament it was “a good day for corporate social responsibility in Canada,” and said, “In the 10 years since the introduction and ultimate defeat of Bill C-300, the Responsible Mining Bill, Canada has evolved from a strong resistance, to naming an ombudsman for the Canadian Office of Responsible Enterprise. This office will help support Canadian companies around the world to operate in accordance with international human rights standards.” Do you think it ever did that at all, or was the CORE really toothless?

JM: Clearly the reports that it actually did were actually quite good. They just didn’t get around to doing too many of them. And I think that they could have been more effective, had they had the authorities that they needed. You have to bear in mind from when I did C-300 to that day [when the CORE was created], it was a long fight, a loooong fight. I guess going from ground zero to maybe a couple rungs up the ladder is always the more difficult part. And yeah, it’s kind of a shame that we fell off the ladder again.

JB: Your 2010 private member’s Bill C-300, the Corporate Accountability of Mining, Oil and Gas Corporations and Developing Countries Act, which was defeated, would have regulated Canadian extractive companies so that they would respect human and environmental rights, and it also would have amended laws that govern Export Development Canada, the Canada Pension Plan, and the Department of Foreign Affairs. That sounds like a bigger and much stronger piece of legislation than what the CORE office actually entailed, much more ambitious that the ombudsperson office?

JM: I think so. When you want to take on somebody or something, you might as well take on everybody. This was definitely David and a big, big Goliath. The Canada Pension people had their knickers in a knot because you were going to be telling them what they could invest in and what they couldn’t … And then GAC [Global Affairs Canada] never likes to be told what to do, especially when they’re doing nothing. The various ambassadors would have been in positions of withdrawing consular support for nasty things that a Canadian mining company might be doing. And that would have been very awkward for them. They don’t like that. And of course, the industry, you would think this was the end of Western civilization, as we know it. And the EDC [Export Development Canada] do not like people telling them what they can invest in and what they can’t. After all, it is their money, not the public’s money. [EDC generates its own revenue from interest, insurance and financing fees]. So, we pretty well covered the entire spectrum of people who would oppose it. Yes, it was an ambitious bill, and that’s probably why some of my friends in the Liberal Party had urgent calls to the washroom or diplomatic flu on the day of the vote.

JB: But Bill C-300 did remarkably well, didn’t it?

JM: Yeah, we came within four or six votes of winning.

JB:  Is that surprising given that it was a private member’s bill and so ambitious, stepping on so many toes?

JM: Well, [Prime Minister Stephen] Harper organized his entire caucus. I think he actually whipped them to be there. But it was a minority government, and the bill had quite a chance of winning. You can never underestimate the hypocrisy of some members of Parliament. We were doing a vote count, and we knew, or we felt, we had a real good chance of winning … a few people had said, “Yes, I’ll support your bill.”

JB: What made you so passionate about this issue of trying to keep Canadian extractive companies working abroad respecting human rights?

JM: I wish I could say I had a Road to Damascus experience or something like that, but I didn’t. I had done a previous private member’s bill on foreign aid and we got it to royal assent, so some people thought I was a private member’s genius. Actually, at that point I had two bills that I got through to royal assent. So you know, I was two and zero, and of course I thought I was a hero. And a guy named Gerry Barr, who was with kind of an umbrella NGO organization [Canadian Council for International Development, now Cooperation Canada], had this idea [for the bill]. I thought it was a good idea, I thought it could actually fly. I certainly don’t move in the same political circles as Gerry does. In fact, the Conservatives used to describe me as the only remaining Conservative in the Liberal caucus, and my orientation would be pro-business.

But to be blunt about it, there’s some business you just can’t do. And if the only way you can make money is by destroying people’s environment or murdering them or raping them, you shouldn’t be in that business. So, I would start off with a fair bit of sympathy to the difficulties in which some mining companies, in particular, would find themselves. But I expect them to say, “Yes, well, if it’s shareholders’ rights versus murdering this person, then I don’t think we should be respecting shareholders’ rights.” In some respects, it’s a moral statement as well. I don’t want to get all religious on you, but I hope a Christian conscience counts for something.

JB: What do you think the loss of the CORE means? Where does this leave people abroad who are suffering as a result of Canadian mining companies in their midst?

JM: I think this falls in the overall context of Canada abandoning its role in countries that are not of economic importance. That’s kind of the downside of the Carney doctrine. It really started with the aid money that we give out. My view is that aid money should have as its primary goal the relief of poverty.

JB: That was your private member’s bill, the 2008 Official Development Assistance Accountability Act, wasn’t it?

JM: Yes, that was the better aid bill. You can go about relieving poverty in several different ways. I just had this conversation with Randeep Sarai [Secretary of State for International Development] a few weeks ago, who was upset about an article I wrote. [That article, “Op-Ed: The problem with the Carney government’s approach to aid: Former MP and creator of aid accountability act says aid effectiveness is diluted when trade becomes the goal,” appeared on May 4, 2026 in Canadian Affairs].

He [Sarai] was pissed off with me because I was criticizing his approach — and this is where it becomes relevant to you — of providing aid money to a mining company so they can train their workers. On the face of it, that seems to be a good idea. But I wouldn’t be taking that money out of aid money. I’d be taking it out of some other program money. I do buy the argument that money can be used to train people. I don’t think the primary focus of your aid money should be what is in Canada’s best interest.

And my argument was that we shouldn’t be giving Warren Buffett [one of the world’s wealthiest people] money either, which is what they did with Tim Hortons. Warren Buffett owns a portion of Tim Hortons. I have a feeling that Warren can pay a few bucks for his own coffee beans. [In his oped, McKay also wrote, “The restaurant chain Tim Hortons has partnered with the Canadian government on a $41-million project to support 50,000 farm families in the Global South. This Coffee for Communities project is half funded by Tim Hortons and half funded by Global Affairs Canada.”]

JB: Do you think that the elimination of the CORE harms Canada’s reputation internationally at all?

JM: I think we’ve done wonderful disservice to our own reputation, because we talk a lot and do nothing. Trudeau was all about anything that fell within the feminist agenda, which ignores half the population, by the way. And it also is an imposition of Western values on other nations, which I think is quite problematic. And again, if Trudeau doesn’t adhere from the left side of the better aid bill, Carney probably doesn’t adhere to it on the right side of the better aid bill. The imposition of your agenda on somebody else who needs money seems a little off to me. And similarly, with somebody from the Carney side. I don’t think either of them got it right. And so, I think it’s had the effect of diminishing our influence in the world. You know, the old phrase was, “The world needs more of Canada.” Meh, I’m not convinced about that. I think Canada could use a bit more of its image of itself. We live in a bit of a la-la land of self-aggrandizing.

JB: The Carney government is cutting $2.7 billion in foreign aid over the next four years?

JM: It’s hard to say you’re expanding your influence when you’re cutting it. And this is, again, another criticism. If you want to have foreign influence abroad, you have the three D’s: defence, diplomacy, and development. We’re certainly going wholeheartedly into defence. Development? I don’t think that the development or the GAC [Global Affairs Canada] budget got increased. And you’ve rolled foreign aid into GAC, and you’re cutting it back. I don’t quite see how you’re going to be increasing your influence abroad by, in effect, cutting off two out of the three legs on a stool.

JB: If you were invited to see the prime minister, what would you say to him about the cutting of the CORE and cutting of foreign aid?

JM: I would challenge him on a re-think. I would say, “Look Mark, I agree entirely with your Davos [World Economic Forum] speech. We need to reduce our dependency on the declining hegemon that is rapidly declining into a failed empire. And we need to join up with like-minded nations. But it’s not just on trade and defence. It is on the other, the phrase is “soft power.” We also need to promote our embassies, and we need to, in the process of supporting our industries abroad, we need also to support those not-for-profit and NGO entities abroad as well.”

JB: If you had run in the 2025 election, and you were in Mark Carney’s caucus, do you think that the CORE would have been eliminated, or do you think the CORE might have got the powers and the new ombudsperson it needed, and done the job that you wanted it to do?

JM: Well, my guess is that they would have got a bit more of a fight. Whether you can change trajectory, I don’t really know. They would at least have known that in caucus was a CORE advocate and maybe we’d have been able to do some other stuff with it. I don’t really know.

Joan Baxter is an award-winning Nova Scotian journalist and author of seven books, including "The Mill: Fifty Years of Pulp and Protest." In October 2024 she was named a member of the International Consortium...
